prohibited_recommendations: Do not give corticosteroids as monotherapy.
required_recommendations: Intubate and mechanically ventilate; ICU admission.
Continuous cardiac telemetry for autonomic instability.

avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Functional / metabolic brain imaging adds no value in a peripheral demyelinating syndrome.
Cerebrovascular imaging is not indicated in a peripheral neuropathy without focal cerebral signs.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

accepted: Guillain-Barré syndrome, severe AIDP (post-influenza A) with respiratory failure

differential.key_features: Cannot distinguish at <8 weeks; longitudinal reassessment.
Axonal features on EMG and ganglioside antibody positivity warrant repeat EMG and serology.
ICU course raises risk but GBS pattern with CSF dissociation precedes ICU stay.

key_clinical_evidence: Severe AIDP with respiratory failure mandates ICU and ventilation.
Autonomic monitoring is mandatory throughout the acute phase.
Repeat EMG at 1–2 weeks for prognostication and AIDP-vs-axonal-variant clarification.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

patient.chief_complaint: Six-day progressive ascending weakness and areflexia with bilateral facial weakness, preceded by URI. SpO2 93% on room air in 68-year-old diabetic.

family_history: Hypertension in family; no neurological disease

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. N. is a 68-year-old man presenting with a 6-day history of progressive ascending weakness. He had a URI 2 weeks ago. Six days ago, foot tingling began; weakness rapidly ascended and he is now unable to walk. He has bilateral facial drooping and cannot swallow water without coughing. SpO2 93% on room air at triage. He has known mild diabetic peripheral neuropathy (distal vibration loss only) — but his new symptoms are acutely different and far more severe.

neurological_exam.additional: FVC: 1.6 L (predicted 3.8 L — 42%). NIF: -22 cmH2O — at threshold. Background mild DPN noted in chart 1 year ago.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral lower motor neuron facial weakness — symmetric, forehead involved. Mild dysarthria. Diminished gag. Dysphagia to thin liquids.
neurological_exam.motor: Marked bilateral lower extremity weakness: hip flexion 2/5, knee extension 3/5, ankle dorsiflexion 2/5. Upper extremity: shoulder abduction 3+/5, grip 4/5.
neurological_exam.sensory: Bilateral glove-and-stocking paresthesias extending to knees.
